figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
FIGURE 1    |    Computational design of the acyl acceptor substrate pocket of DBATcus. (a) The docking result of MODEL1 and DT performed using 
AutoDock Vina. The gridbox was centered on the catalytic residues of DBATcus, and the optimal binding conformation was selected based on the 
lowest docking score and interactions. The three-­dimensional structure of MODEL1 is shown as cartoon, the 37 ‘hotspots’ for virtual saturation mu­
tation are coloured in marine and shown as transparent surface, the evolutionarily highly conserved sites (the Consurf score ≥ 8) are shown in pink, 
and the substrate DT is shown as yellow sticks. (b) The enzyme specific activities and biomass activities of DBATcus virtual mutants against DT and 
10-­DAB, respectively. (c) The spatial position of the high activity mutation sites. The amino acids are displayed as marine sticks. The substrate DT is 
shown as yellow sticks. (d) The temperature curves of DBATcus and its mutants toward DT. (e) The pH curves of DBATcus and its mutants toward DT. 
(f–j) Enzymatic kinetic parameters of DBATcus, P217K, E350M, S351D and S396G toward DT. The kinetic parameters were determined with a series 
of substrate concentrations (15.625–2000 μM DT) under each optimum condition of the protein. Kinetic parameters (Km, Vmax and kcat) were calcu­
lated by fitting the initial velocity data to the Michaelis-­Menten equation using nonlinear regression analysis. All assays were performed in triplicate 
(n = 3) with independent experiments. Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD).Figure 1[BB:45.3543307086614;426.03739

figure_candidates.caption:
FIGURE 3    |    Construction and determination of DNA shuffling mutants. (a) The 21 differential residue sites among six DBATs. (b) Localization of 
the 21 residues in the three-­dimensional structure of DBATcus. The DT substrate was docked into the active pocket using AutoDock Vina as described 
in Figure 1 and shown as yellow sticks. The 21 residues were shown as spheres. The scale of the sphere was set to 0.8. (c) Flow chart of DNA shuffling 
mutant strain screening. 459 colonies were collected from the LB plates, and 323 positive transformants were screened by colony PCR. Cellular-­level 
catalysis of 10-­DAB showed that 86 transformants were active, of which 17 exhibited higher activity than wild-­type DBATcus. (d) The 17 DNA shuf­
fling mutants with increased biomass activity toward 10-­DAB. (e) DNA shuffling mutants with significantly increased specific activity toward DT 
and their mutation sites. Except for SF-­80, the other eight mutants all contain the R345C mutation.Figure 3[BB:45.3543307086614;487.4

FIGURE 4    |    Molecular mechanism analysis of DBATcus and R345C. (a) The hydrogen bond network of R345 in DBATcus. DT is shown as yellow 
sticks, R345 is shown as pink sticks, residues that form hydrogen bonds directly with R345 are shown as cyan sticks, and residues that form hydro­
